newsitem.title: USA: Florida judge rules electric chair not cruel.
newsitem.headline: Florida judge rules electric chair not cruel.

text.p: A Florida judge on Friday turned back a constitutional challenge to Florida's malfunctioning electric chair, ruling it did not constitute cruel and unusual punishment.

Circuit Judge A.C. Soud concluded that Pedro Medina, the death row inmate whose fiery execution in March sparked a lengthy inquiry into the condition of the 74-year-old chair, died instantly and did not suffer conscious pain.

Flames leaped from the headpiece of the execution apparatus during Medina's execution and an acrid smoke filled the death chamber. It was the second time in 10 years the chair -- nicknamed "Old Sparky" -- produced fire during an execution.
"He (Medina) suffered no conscious pain," Soud said as he read from his 25-page ruling Friday. "This can be said for all inmates who will be executed in Florida's electric chair."

The Florida Supreme Court in May suspended executions until at least September to allow a thorough court review of the electric chair, which death penalty opponents have argued is unconstitutionally cruel. The high court has scheduled hearings of its own for September.

At a hearing before Soud last week, researcher Donald Price, a Medical College of Virginia expert on brains and pain testified there was a "high likelihood that judicial execution by electrocution is excruciatingly and intensely painful."
Experts called by the state said the chair, which produces a 2,000-volt jolt, kills immediately and without pain.

Soud concluded that the flames during Medina's execution resulted from human error -- a failure to properly wet a sponge used in the headpiece. He recommended that executioners increase the salinity of the solution used to soak the sponge.
Leo Alexander Jones, the death row inmate next in line for execution, was in court Friday but showed no emotion at the ruling. His execution was delayed until at least Sept. 15.
Jones was convicted for the 1981 sniper killing of a Jacksonville police officer. His daughter, Chennelle Jones, 25, said she was not surprised by the ruling but declined further comment.
